---
title: "Getting started"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 3.6, out.width = "100%")
```

cppDE writes C++ code for a model given as equations in R, compiles it
and runs it: `cppODE()` and `cvode()` for ordinary differential
equations, `cppFUN()` for algebraic functions. Derivatives in the
parameters come with the values, forward or reverse, to first and second
order. This page goes through the entry points on small models; the
[methods](methods-codegen.html) describe what the generated code does.

## Requirements

Code is generated and compiled at run time, so a C++17 compiler and
Python with SymPy are needed; `codegenAvailable()` checks both, and
`codegenAvailable("cvode")` whether cppDE was installed with SUNDIALS.
Every model below is compiled into `tempdir()`, the default `outdir`.

```{r library, message = FALSE}
library(cppDE)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))

codegenAvailable()
codegenAvailable("cvode")
```

The figures show a trajectory and its sensitivities as one long data
frame, one panel per state and per derivative of a state:

```{r longFormat}
longFormat <- function(out, states = colnames(out$variable), sens = TRUE) {
  nt <- length(out$time)
  value <- data.frame(time = out$time, panel = rep(states, each = nt),
                      value = as.vector(out$variable[, states]))
  if (!sens) return(value)
  tangent <- out$tangent[, states, , drop = FALSE]
  grid <- expand.grid(time = out$time, state = states,
                      par = dimnames(tangent)[[3]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  rbind(value, data.frame(time = grid$time,
                          panel = sprintf("d%s/d%s", grid$state, grid$par),
                          value = as.vector(tangent)))
}
```

## A first model

A decay chain $A \to B$. `cppODE()` generates the solver and compiles it;
`solveODE()` returns the states and, by default, their derivatives in
every initial value and parameter.

```{r chain}
eqns  <- c(A = "-k1*A", B = "k1*A - k2*B")
parms <- c(A = 1, B = 0, k1 = 0.5, k2 = 0.2)
times <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.1)

chain <- cppODE(eqns, modelname = "chain")
out   <- solveODE(chain, times, parms)

dim(out$tangent)                       # [time, state, parameter]
out$tangent[101, "B", ]                # dB(10) / d(A, B, k1, k2)
```

```{r chain-plot, fig.height = 4.2}
ggplot(longFormat(out), aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 5)
```

`method` selects the integrator: `"bdf"` (the default, NDF formulas),
`"adams"`, the Rosenbrock method `"rb4"` or the explicit Runge-Kutta pair
`"tsit5"`. `?expressions` lists what an equation can contain.

## Several models in one shared object

A model generated with `compile = FALSE` is only written to disk;
`compile()` then builds several of them into one shared object. The
models of the following sections are generated here and compiled
together.

```{r generate}
chain2 <- cppODE(eqns, deriv2 = TRUE, modelname = "chain2", compile = FALSE)
chainR <- cppODE(eqns, derivMode = "reverse", modelname = "chainR", compile = FALSE)

events <- data.frame(var = c("A", "A"), time = c("t_e", NA), value = c("dose", "dose"),
                     method = c("add", "add"), root = c(NA, "A - Amin"))
dosed  <- cppODE(eqns, events = events, modelname = "dosed", compile = FALSE)

pulse  <- cppODE(c(A = "u*(time >= t1 && time < t2) - k1*A", B = "k1*A - k2*B"),
                 modelname = "pulse", compile = FALSE)
slide  <- cppODE(c(x = "-k*x + p*(x < xc)"), modelname = "slide", compile = FALSE)
forced <- cppODE(c(A = "u - k1*A", B = "k1*A - k2*B"), forcings = "u",
                 modelname = "forced", compile = FALSE)
steady <- cppODE(c(A = "k0 - k1*A", B = "k1*A - k2*B"), rootfunc = "equilibrate",
                 modelname = "steady", compile = FALSE)

enzyme <- c(E  = "-kon*E*S + (koff + kcat)*ES",
            S  = "-kon*E*S + koff*ES + kback*P",
            ES = " kon*E*S - (koff + kcat)*ES",
            P  = " kcat*ES - kback*P")
enz <- cppFUN(enzyme, variables = names(enzyme),
              parameters = c("kon", "koff", "kcat", "kback"), modelname = "enzyme")
g   <- cppFUN(c(y = "s*(A + B)", z = "log(B)"), variables = c("A", "B"),
              parameters = "s", derivMode = c("forward", "reverse"),
              modelname = "observable")

compile(chain2, chainR, dosed, pulse, slide, forced, steady, enz, g,
        output = "gettingStarted", cores = 2)
```

## Second order

`deriv2 = TRUE` adds the Hessian of every state in the initial values and
parameters.

```{r second-order}
out2 <- solveODE(chain2, times, parms)
out2$hessian[101, "B", , ]             # Hessian of B(10)
```

## Reverse mode

`derivMode = "reverse"` returns the gradient of a weighted sum of the
states, `sum(cotangent * x)`, in one backward sweep, at a cost
independent of the number of parameters. The cotangent below weights $B$
at $t = 10$ only, so the gradient is the row $\partial B(10) / \partial
(A, B, k_1, k_2)$ from above.

```{r reverse}
w <- matrix(0, length(times), 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("A", "B")))
w[101, "B"] <- 1
solveODE(chainR, times, parms, cotangent = w)$cotangent
```

The gradient of a least-squares objective: the cotangent holds the
residuals. `keepStore = TRUE` keeps the forward pass, so that a further
cotangent at the same parameters costs one backward sweep and no
integration.

```{r reverse-ls}
data <- data.frame(time = times, B = 0.4 * exp(-0.3 * times) * (1 - exp(-times)))
first <- solveODE(chainR, times, parms, keepStore = TRUE)
res   <- first$variable[, "B"] - data$B
w[]   <- 0
w[, "B"] <- 2 * res
solveODE(chainR, times, parms, cotangent = w, store = first$store)$cotangent
2 * colSums(res * out$tangent[, "B", ])          # the same from forward mode
```

The two agree to the integration tolerance: each mode returns the exact
derivative of its own discretisation, see the
[discrete adjoint](methods-reverse.html).

## Events

Events are a data frame: which state, when or on which root, which value,
and how it is applied (`"replace"`, `"add"`, `"multiply"`). Here a dose is
added at the time `t_e` and whenever $A$ falls to `Amin`. The
sensitivities take each jump, also where a parameter moves the event
time.

```{r events, fig.height = 2.4}
outE <- solveODE(dosed, times, c(parms, t_e = 2, dose = 1, Amin = 0.3), maxroot = 3)

ggplot(longFormat(outE, "A"), aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4)
```

## Switches

Comparisons and `piecewise()` switch the right-hand side. The solver
locates the switch as a root, so a short pulse is not stepped over. Below,
a pulse of inflow into $A$ between `t1` and `t2`.

```{r pulse, fig.height = 4.2}
outP <- solveODE(pulse, times, c(A = 0, B = 0, k1 = 0.5, k2 = 0.2, u = 1, t1 = 1,
                                 t2 = 1.5))

ggplot(longFormat(outP, "B"), aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4)
```

A switch on a state. Above `xc`, $x$ decays; below, an inflow
`p > k*xc` pushes it back up. Both branches move onto $x = x_c$, so $x$
slides along it, and from then on its only sensitivity is the one in
`xc`.

```{r slide, fig.height = 2.4}
outS <- solveODE(slide, times, c(x = 2, k = 1, p = 3, xc = 1))

ggplot(longFormat(outS), aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 5)
```

## Forcings

A forcing is an input given as data when solving. Between its points it
is interpolated monotonically.

```{r forcings, fig.height = 2.4}
u    <- list(u = data.frame(time = seq(0, 10, by = 0.5),
                            value = 1 + sin(seq(0, 10, by = 0.5))))
outF <- solveODE(forced, times, parms, forcings = u)

ggplot(longFormat(outF, sens = FALSE), aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y")
```

## Steady states

`rootfunc = "equilibrate"` integrates until every derivative is
negligible and returns the steady state with its sensitivities, here
$A = k_0/k_1$ and $B = k_0/k_2$.

```{r equilibrate}
outQ <- solveODE(steady, c(0, 1e4), c(parms, k0 = 1), abstol = 1e-10,
                 reltol = 1e-10, roottol = 1e-10)
tail(outQ$time, 1)
tail(outQ$variable, 1)
outQ$tangent[nrow(outQ$variable), , ]
```

`ptc()` solves for the steady state directly, by pseudo-transient
continuation, with the conservation laws of the system as constraints.
The right-hand side is a `cppFUN()` object; the rows of `C` are the
conserved totals $E + ES$ and $S + ES + P$.

```{r ptc}
C <- rbind(Etot = c(E = 1, S = 0, ES = 1, P = 0),
           Stot = c(E = 0, S = 1, ES = 1, P = 1))
ss <- ptc(enz, x = c(E = 1, S = 1, ES = 1, P = 1),
          parms = c(kon = 1, koff = 0.5, kcat = 0.3, kback = 0.1),
          C = C, total = c(1, 10))
ss$x
```

## Algebraic functions

`cppFUN()` compiles functions of variables and parameters with their
derivatives, here an observable of the decay chain. The Jacobian is in
the variables and parameters together; `evaluate()` returns value and
derivatives from one pass, and `vjp()` contracts a cotangent of the
outputs in one reverse sweep.

```{r cppFUN}
g$func(A = 0.2, B = 0.5, s = 2)
g$jac(A = 0.2, B = 0.5, s = 2)[1, , ]

# the observable on the solved trajectory, and the gradient of sum(y)
x <- out$variable[, c("A", "B")]
v <- g$vjp(vars = x, params = c(s = 2),
           cotangent = cbind(y = rep(1, nrow(x)), z = 0))
v$cotangentP
```

## Batches of conditions

`solveODEBatch()` solves several conditions of one model in one call, in
parallel over OpenMP threads where cppDE was built with OpenMP
(`batchAvailable()`). The result of each condition is that of
`solveODE()`, bit for bit.

```{r batch}
conditions <- list(slow = list(parms = c(A = 1, B = 0, k1 = 0.2, k2 = 0.2)),
                   fast = list(parms = c(A = 1, B = 0, k1 = 2, k2 = 0.2)))
batch <- solveODEBatch(chain, conditions, times = times, cores = 2)
sapply(batch, function(r) r$variable[101, ])
```

An optimiser solves the same conditions many times with new parameters.
`prepareBatch()` converts the arguments once; `solveBatch()` then takes
only the new numbers, in the order of the prepared conditions.

```{r prepared}
h <- prepareBatch(chain, conditions, times = times)
again <- solveBatch(h, parms = list(c(A = 1, B = 0, k1 = 0.3, k2 = 0.1),
                                    c(A = 1, B = 0, k1 = 3, k2 = 0.1)), cores = 2)
sapply(again, function(r) r$tangent[101, "B", ])
```

## The cvode() backend

`cvode()` compiles the same equations against SUNDIALS CVODES, if cppDE
was installed with it, see `?installLibs`. It takes the same arguments
and returns a model for the same `solveODE()`; its sensitivities are the
CVODES forward sensitivities or, with `derivMode = "reverse"`, its
adjoint. The [comparison](methods-cvode.html) lists what differs.

```{r cvode, eval = codegenAvailable("cvode")}
chainC <- cvode(eqns, deriv = TRUE, modelname = "chainC")
outC   <- solveODE(chainC, times, parms, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
outN   <- solveODE(chain, times, parms, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
max(abs(outC$tangent - outN$tangent))
```

## Further

Two articles go further:
[Sensitivities across events, checked symbolically](saltation.html) compares forward and
reverse sensitivities across events, switches and sliding with symbolic solutions to second
order, and [Fitting magnetisation dynamics](fitCoPt.html) fits a Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert model
to pump-probe measurements by Gauss-Newton on forward sensitivities, with a moving-average noise
model, a multistart and profile likelihoods.

[dMod2](https://dmodverse.github.io/dMod2/) builds observation functions,
parameter transformations, objectives, optimisers and profile likelihoods
on cppDE.
